'''Eli Yablonovitch''' (born 15 December 1946) is an American [[physicist]] and engineer who, along with [[Sajeev John]], founded the field of [[photonic crystal]]s in 1987.<ref name=":0">M.Kapoor (2013) [http://shodhganga.inflibnet.ac.in/bitstream/10603/7246/5/chapter_3.pdf Electromagnetic Band Gap Structures], page 58</ref> He and his team were the first to create a 3-dimensional structure that exhibited a full [[photonic bandgap]], which has been named [[Yablonovite]]. In addition to pioneering photonic crystals, he was the first to recognize that a [[strained quantum-well laser]] has a significantly reduced threshold current compared to its unstrained counterpart. This is now employed in the majority of [[semiconductor laser]]s fabricated throughout the world. His seminal paper<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Yablonovitch|first=Eli|date=1987-05-18|title=Inhibited Spontaneous Emission in Solid-State Physics and Electronics|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=58|issue=20|pages=2059–2062|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059|pmid=10034639|bibcode=1987PhRvL..58.2059Y|doi-access=free}}</ref> reporting inhibited [[spontaneous emission]] in photonic crystals is among the most highly cited papers in physics and [[engineering]].

==Career==
Yablonovitch received his [[Bachelor of Science|B.Sc.]] in physics from [[McGill University]] in 1967.  He went on to receive his [[Master of Arts|A.M.]] degree in applied physics from [[Harvard University]] in 1969, and his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] from Harvard in 1972.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title = Eli Yablonovitch {{!}} EECS at UC Berkeley|url = https://www.eecs.berkeley.edu/Faculty/Homepages/yablonovitch.html|website = www.eecs.berkeley.edu|access-date = 2016-01-08}}</ref> During his post-graduate studies, Yablonovitch worked on [[nonlinear optics]] with [[carbon dioxide laser]]s.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url = http://optoelectronics.eecs.berkeley.edu/ResumeStd.pdf|title = Curriculum Vitae|last = Yablonovitch|first = Eli}}</ref>

After receiving his Ph.D., Yablonovitch worked at [[Bell Labs|Bell Laboratories]].  He then became a professor of applied physics at Harvard in 1974.  In 1979, he joined [[ExxonMobil|Exxon research center]] to work on photovoltaic research for solar energy.<ref name=":2" /> While working at Exxon, Yablonovitch derived the 4 (n squared) factor as the theoretical limit for light trapping in photovoltaics. This is now used worldwide in almost all solar panels.<ref name=":1" />

Yablonovitch joined [[Bell Communications Research]] in 1984, and became its director of solid-state physics research in 1991. During his time at Bell Communications, Yablonovitch did his pioneering work on [[photonic crystal]]s.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" />

Yablonovitch became a professor of [[electrical engineering]] at [[UCLA]] and continued to study and develop [[photonic crystal]]s and [[Photonic-bandgap fiber|photonic bandgap materials]]. In July 2007, he joined the Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences department at [[UC Berkeley]]. His research topics include [[silicon photonics]], [[telecommunications]], optical [[Antenna (radio)|antennas]], new applications of [[photovoltaics]], and searching for a low-voltage replacement for the transistor. Recently he has investigated analog computing approaches to solving hard problems, such as the [[traveling salesman problem]].

== Entrepreneurship ==
Yablonovitch has co-founded multiple companies related to his research interests. In 2000, he co-founded Ethertronics Inc. Ethertronics is a cell phone antenna manufacturer that has, to date, shipped over 1.7 billion antennas.<ref name=":2" />

In 2001, Yablonovitch co-founded [[Luxtera|Luxtera Inc.]], a semiconductor company that makes electro‑optical systems using silicon photonics, manufactured with [[CMOS]] processes. [[Luxtera]] is the first company to market foundry-based [[silicon photonics]].<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web|title = FIBER OPTICS: Optical transceiver goes where copper cannot|url = http://www.laserfocusworld.com/articles/print/volume-43/issue-9/world-news/fiber-optics-optical-transceiver-goes-where-copper-cannot.html|website = www.laserfocusworld.com| date=September 2007 |access-date = 2016-01-08}}</ref>

Yablonovitch co-founded Luminescent Inc. in 2002.  Luminescent provided sophisticated mathematical optimization for use in photolithography masks.   Luminescent was acquired by [[Synopsys]] in 2012.<ref name=":2" />

In 2008, Yablonovitch founded Alta Devices Inc.  Alta Devices produces thin-film [[gallium arsenide]] photovoltaic cells for solar energy.  Alta Devices currently holds the efficiency world record for single junction solar cells at 29.1% and dual junction solar cells at 31.6%, both at 1 sun illumination.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.altadevices.com/about/|title = The Alta Story| date=10 January 2023 }}</ref>

== Fellowships and awards ==
He is a Fellow of the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE), the [[Optica (society)|Optical Society of America]] (OSA), and the [[American Physical Society]] (APS).

He was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]], the [[National Academy of Engineering]], the [[National Academy of Inventors]], the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and a [[Foreign Member of the Royal Society|Foreign Member of the Royal Society of London]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/about-us/fellowship/new-fellows-2013/|title=New Fellows 2013|publisher=Royal Society|access-date = 30 July 2013}}</ref>

He is a recipient of the:

* 1978 [[Adolph Lomb Medal]];
* 1993 W. Streifer Scientific Achievement Award;<ref>{{Cite web |title=William Streifer Scientific Achievement Award |url=https://ieeephotonics.org/awards/william-streifer-scientific-achievement-award/ |access-date=2023-07-25 |website=The IEEE Photonics Society |language=en-US}}</ref>
* 1996 [[R. W. Wood Prize]];
* 2001 [[Julius Springer]] Prize;<ref>{{Cite web |title=Applied Physics B |url=https://www.springer.com/journal/340/updates/17188340 |access-date=2023-07-25 |website=Springer |language=en}}</ref>
* 2010 [[Mountbatten Medal]] of the [[Institution of Engineering and Technology]] (IET);
* 2011 [[List of Clarivate Citation laureates in Physics|Clarivate Citation laureate in Physics]], shared with [[Sajeev John]], "for their invention and development of [[Photonic crystals|photonic band gap materials]].";<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Thomson Reuters Predicts Nobel Laureates |url=https://www.acnnewswire.com/press-release/english/7559/thomson-reuters-predicts-nobel-laureates |access-date=2023-10-04 |website=www.acnnewswire.com}}</ref>
* 2012 [[IEEE Photonics Award]];
* 2012 [[Harvey Prize]];
* 2014 [[Rank Prizes|Rank Prize for Optoelectronics]];
* 2015 [[Isaac Newton Medal]] by [[Institute of Physics]];<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=2015 Isaac Newton medal of the Institute of Physics |url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/newton/page_65856.html |access-date=2016-01-08 |website=www.iop.org}}</ref>
* 2016 [[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize]];
* 2017 [[IEEE William R. Cherry Award]]—the IEEE's highest award in solar cells;<ref>{{Cite web |title=2017 IEEE PVSC-44 {{!}} Washington, DC |url=http://www.ieee-pvsc.org/PVSC44/awards-cherry.php |access-date=2017-03-28 |website=www.ieee-pvsc.org |language=en}}</ref>
* 2018 [[IEEE Edison Medal]];
* 2019 [[Frederic Ives Medal | Frederic Ives Medal / Jarus W. Quinn Prize]]—the [[Optical Society]]'s highest award;
* 2019 [[Benjamin Franklin Medal (Franklin Institute)|Benjamin Franklin medal]].
